claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in RAFM steels is governed by the interplay of mobile dislocation networks, nanoscale precipitates, and a bimodal microstructure.
High-temperature toughness in RAFM steels is governed by the same interplay of mobile dislocation networks, nanoscale precipitates, and a bimodal microstructure.
The proposed microstructure promotes continuous dislocation transfer.
The proposed microstructure delays crack initiation under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Conventionally processed RAFM steel has coarser grains and a lower density of nanoscale precipitates than the modified material.
A modified thermomechanical process can produce refined ferritic and tempered-martensitic microstructural features, fine subgrains, and a high density of nanoscale precipitates in RAFM steel.
The modified thermomechanical process promotes a high mobile-dislocation population in ferrite.
The relevant structural mediator is a bimodal or multiscale microstructure containing fine grains, fine subgrains, and a high density of nanoscale precipitates.
Nanoscale precipitates act as barriers that accumulate dislocations.
After accumulating dislocations, nanoscale precipitates facilitate their migration across subgrain boundaries.
High mobile-dislocation density in ferrite, subgrain formation in tempered martensite, and the bimodal microstructure enhance ductility.
The proposed dislocation mechanism delays strain localization that would otherwise lead to crack initiation.
Relative to conventionally processed RAFM steel, modified RAFM steel will have greater plastic strain before failure at temperatures above 600 °C under simulated irradiation.
Relative to conventionally processed RAFM steel, modified RAFM steel will have improved fracture toughness at temperatures above 600 °C under simulated irradiation.
Higher precipitate density and enhanced dislocation structures will correlate with improved mechanical performance.
Conventionally processed RAFM steel exhibits more pronounced high-temperature strain localization than the modified material.
The proposed mechanism applies under fusion conditions above 600 °C with neutron- or helium-related irradiation effects.
The mechanism may not generalize to materials with chemistries or microstructural modifications outside RAFM steels.
